    Industry News: Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

    📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt.
    • Recent findings suggest that high-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago.
    • Sources indicate that the high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

    Recent findings suggest that high-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

    Sources indicate that the high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

    Sources indicate that spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

    The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

    Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," stated Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

    It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

    Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

    "The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

    He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

    That mentioned, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

    It has been revealed that "There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning.".

    While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

    In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

    "We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

    The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, stated Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

    Sources indicate that the overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he mentioned. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market.".

    Sources indicate that in addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

    The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she mentioned.

    It has been revealed that "It is isolated," she remarked. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now.".

    For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

    "We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she stated.

    Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

    But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

    Recent findings suggest that "We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising.".

    Industry observers note that it's also notable to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, remarked R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

    "With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

    High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

    "That's when spreads really widen out," he noted. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder.".

    Charging to 100% Every Night Wears Down Your Phone’s Battery. Try This Instead

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that apple states iPhone batteries are most comfortable at temperatures between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit, and charging outside that range, whether in a hot car or inside a thick case, speeds up wear.
    • Voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss.
    • According to recent reports, age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that apple states iPhone batteries are most comfortable at temperatures between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit, and charging outside that range, whether in a hot car or inside a thick case, speeds up wear. Heat is one of two things that age a phone battery faster than normal use. The other is time spent at 100%. Avoiding both takes very little effort, and the charge limit settings on iPhones, Pixels and Galaxy phones handle part of the job for you. Here’s how to charge in a way that keeps your battery healthier for longer.

    Voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss. The damage may not appear immediately, but it’s measurable after one year and obvious after two.

    According to recent reports, age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably. Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity faster when they spend extended time at the top of their charge range, which is precisely where an overnight charge leaves them. The fix doesn’t require a fresh phone or even a new charger. It requires a small adjustment to a habit most people have never thought twice about.

    In a recent development, keeping a lithium-ion cell pinned at 100% creates voltage stress, and the heat generated from sitting on a charger could end up meaning the difference between keeping your current phone a little longer or having to buy a latest one. So once and for all, does keeping your phone plugged in really hurt the battery? Here’s what the experts suggest.

    It has been revealed that it isn’t about immediate damage but rather how fast your battery ages over time. Understanding the difference between what will and won’t break your phone is key. Here is the truth about your charging habits.

    In a recent development, battery health is not just about how many times you charge your phone. It is also about how it manages voltage, temperature and maintenance. Lithium-ion batteries age fastest when they are exposed to extreme levels: 0% and 100%.

    Keeping these batteries near full charge for long stretches of time puts additional voltage stress on the cathode and electrolyte. This is why many devices use “trickle charging” or temporarily pause at 100%, topping up only when needed.

    Still, the biggest threat is not overcharging, but heat. When your phone is plugged in and running demanding apps, it produces heat that accelerates chemical wear inside the battery. If you are gaming, streaming or charging on a hot day, that extra warmth does far more harm than leaving the cable plugged in overnight.

    According to recent reports, the Apple battery guide describes lithium-ion batteries as “consumable components” that naturally lose capacity over time. To slow that decline, iPhones use Optimized Battery Charging, which learns your daily routine and pauses charging at about 80% until just before you typically unplug, reducing time spent at high voltage.

    Apple also advises keeping devices between 0 and 35 degrees Celsius (32 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit) and removing certain cases while charging to improve heat dissipation. You can read more on the official Apple battery support page.

    Sources indicate that samsung offers a similar feature called Battery Protect, found in the One UI battery and device care settings. When enabled, it caps charging at 85%, which helps reduce stress during long charging sessions.

    Industry observers note that other Android makers like Google, OnePlus and Xiaomi include comparable options — often called Adaptive Charging, Optimized Charging or Battery Care — that dynamically slow power delivery or limit charge based on your habits. These systems make it safe to leave your phone plugged in for extended periods without fear of overcharging.

    Even with these safeguards, some conditions can accelerate battery wear. As mentioned before, the most common culprit is high temperatures. Even for a short period of time, leaving your phone charging in direct sunlight, in a car or under a pillow can push temperatures into unsafe zones.

    Heavy use, such as gaming or 4K video editing, while charging can also cause temperature spikes which can degrade the battery faster. And cheap, uncertified cables or adapters may deliver unstable current that stresses cells. If your battery is already several years old, it will naturally be more sensitive to this kind of strain.

    Industry observers note that there is no need to overhaul your habits, but a few tweaks can help your battery age gracefully. Start by turning on the optimization tools on your phone: Optimized Battery Charging on iPhones, Battery Protect on Samsung devices and Adaptive Charging on Google Pixels. These systems learn your routine and adjust charging speed so your phone is not sitting at 100% all night.

    Keep your phone cool while charging. According to Apple, phone batteries perform best between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit (16 to 22 degrees Celsius). If your phone feels hot, remove its case or move it to a better ventilated or shaded spot. Avoid tossing your phone under a pillow or too close to other electronics, like your laptop. Skip wireless chargers that trap heat overnight. Use quality chargers and cables from your phone manufacturer or trusted brands. Those cheap “fast-charge” kits you find online often deliver inconsistent current, which can cause long-term issues.

    Finally, try not to obsess over topping off the charge. It is perfectly fine to plug in your phone during the day for short bursts. Lithium-ion batteries actually prefer frequent, shallow charges rather than deep full cycles. There is no need to keep it between 20% and 80% all the time, but just avoid extremes when possible.

    Keeping your phone plugged in overnight or on your desk all day will not destroy its battery. That is a leftover myth from a different era of tech. Modern phones are smart enough to protect themselves, and features such as Optimized Battery Charging or Battery Protect do most of the heavy lifting for you.

    It has been revealed that still, no battery lasts forever. The best way to slow the inevitable is to manage heat, use quality chargers and let the software on your phone do its job. Think of it less as “babying” your battery and more as charging with intention. A few mindful habits today can keep your phone running strong for years to come.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By John Ballard – Nov 23, 2026 at 10:22AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    Sources indicate that nvidia (NVDA +31.21%), the designer of the graphics chips that power AI data centers, just got its founder back. On Nov. 23, the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after the manufacturer announced his resignation.

    The stock has whipsawed in November. It closed trading on Nov. 20 at about 48% below its 52-week high on Oct. 6. Following the news of Huang’s reinstatement on Monday, the shares were up over 30% from Friday's close but still about 32% below that October high.

    It has been revealed that huang's return settles the biggest question hanging over the stock, while the business never slowed down. Here's why Nvidia still looks like a buy.

    NASDAQ · As of 11:49 AM ET 11/23/26.

    Huang understands graphics chip technology and the dynamics of the chip industry as well as anyone. He built Nvidia around CUDA, the software platform that lets developers run programs on its chips, which keeps customers locked into Nvidia's hardware. When Nvidia partnered with Intel in 2025, Huang described CUDA as the center of AI's reinvention of computing.

    Recent findings suggest that he is also a skilled dealmaker. On Oct. 27, just weeks before his brief exit, Nvidia agreed to invest $3 billion in an equity offering by Meta Platforms, while Meta said it would expand its use of Nvidia's newest Vera Rubin systems and Spectrum-X networking. Deals like that help keep Nvidia at the center of its biggest customers' prepares, even as some of those customers develop their own chips.

    Huang built Nvidia into the most notable technology tech giant to the global economy. It is the dominant leader in graphics processing units (GPUs), which remain the workhorse chips for AI workloads. With its founder back in charge and demand still strong, Nvidia is well-positioned to deliver further upside for shareholders.

    It has been revealed that nvidia's results tell a different story than its stock price. Third-quarter revenue jumped 103% from a year ago to $116 billion, driven by a 110% surge in data center sales. Its fresh Vera Rubin platform, a rack-sized AI computer, brought in nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of shipments, the fastest product ramp in company history. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion.

    It has been revealed that nvidia also raised its outlook for next year, now calling for revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% previously. CFO Colette Kress stated that Nvidia's supply agreements now extend to the end of the decade.

    Recent findings suggest that the biggest risk is customer concentration. In fiscal 2026, one direct customer accounted for 22% of revenue, and another accounted for 14%. If either one pulled back on spending, Nvidia's sales and growth could take a significant hit.

    Wall Street expects Nvidia to earn $16.61 per share in fiscal 2028, according to Yahoo! Finance. Even after the Nov. 23 jump, the stock is trading at just over 10 times next year's earnings, an incredibly low multiple for a company still growing this fast. Analysts expect earnings growth of about 49% annualized in the coming years.

    With Huang back, investors no longer have to wonder who will run Nvidia next, and the company doesn't have to replace a visionary founder.

    The remaining watch item is the board's independent investigation, which will proceed to its conclusion. The board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to oversee trade compliance. If the review turns up newly introduced problems, the stock could swing sharply again. Still, the board said it is confident, based on input from senior U.S. government officials, that Huang's return poses no national security risk.

    I believe Nvidia stock is worth buying at this price, given its growth and low valuation. What Huang built over the last 30-plus years won’t fade away anytime soon, and he's back to keep building it. Nvidia's momentum is strong, which should benefit the stock in 2027 and beyond.

    If you're here looking for lower mortgage interest rates, today is definitely not your day.

    The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.38% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points higher than yesterday and 12 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    Keep in mind that mortgage rates are always on the move, and that if you're tracking rates day-to-day, you're going to see a lot of volatility. Zooming out and looking at the bigger picture — like a graph showing at least a month's worth of rate data — can help you see the overall trend.

    Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:.

    » Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

    It has been revealed that mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

    Recent findings suggest that on Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

    The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

    Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

    » MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates.

    Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you blueprint to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

    With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.88% or higher — but there aren’t many people for whom that’s true.

    It has been revealed that also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

    If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

    According to recent reports, » Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

    There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

    Sources indicate that if the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

    According to recent reports, nerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a upcoming home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings.     #142381. Breaking: 18 Hidden Software Delivery Problems And How To Spot Them

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1379 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 18 Hidden Software Delivery Problems And How To Spot Them

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that software delivery pipelines move code from development through testing and deployment, generating a wealth of data along the way.
    • Identifying these issues early requires looking beyond standard performance metrics to understand how effectively the entire delivery process is working.
    • In data centers, no change touches live equipment without a written procedure and a tested back-out plan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that software delivery pipelines move code from development through testing and deployment, generating a wealth of data along the way. Yet even when engineering teams track metrics such as deployment frequency, build times and failure rates, less obvious problems can undermine software quality, reliability and efficiency.

    Identifying these issues early requires looking beyond standard performance metrics to understand how effectively the entire delivery process is working. Below, Forbes Technology Council members highlight often-overlooked problems in software delivery pipelines and the signals that can help engineering teams detect them.

    In data centers, no change touches live equipment without a written procedure and a tested back-out plan. Software teams rarely meet that standard. The hidden problem is rollback paths nobody has exercised. Track the share of releases whose rollback was actually run in staging before deployment. If that number is low, your safety net is an assumption, not a plan. - Jon Trout, Chekhub.

    In a recent development, I believe the hidden problem is complexity accumulation. Every release adds code, integrations, exceptions and dependencies, while the pipeline continues to report progress. The signal I watch is cognitive load: how many systems, teams, decisions and business rules an engineer must understand to make a safe change. When that number keeps rising, innovation slows, risk compounds and agility erodes long before traditional delivery metrics reveal the problem. - Dr. Suresh Rajappa, KPMG LLP.

    According to recent reports, forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    In a recent development, work waiting in the system is a hidden problem—and one that existed before AI. The revealing signal is low flow efficiency (or, equivalently, high wait time as a percentage of lead time). This is exposed through value-stream metrics like lead and cycle time, PR age, and so on. This also shifts the conversation from, “How do we make engineers code faster?” to, “Why is valuable work standing still?” That is usually where the biggest delivery gains exist. - Jesse Stockall, Flexera.

    Many engineering teams can tell you how quickly they release software, but not how much effort goes into fixing what was just released. That disconnect is often hidden until it starts affecting customers. One signal worth watching is change failure rate. When more deployments lead to incidents, rollbacks or urgent fixes, the problem is rarely a lack of productivity. More often, it’s a sign that quality issues are being discovered too late in the delivery process. - Dzmitry Lubneuski, a1qa.

    It has been revealed that assuming AI-generated code is safe because it passes automated tests is a major blind spot. As pull request volume grows, human reviewers can start succumbing to review fatigue and rubber-stamping changes, allowing security risks and technical debt to slip through. Instead, teams must track hard-to-find bugs, codebase standards and cross-repo impact after code is merged, not just whether tests pass. - Itamar Friedman, Qodo.ai.

    It has been revealed that the hidden problem is communication lag. With AI-assisted workflows, engineering is no longer the bottleneck. We’re shipping far more code and newly introduced work than internal and customer-facing teams can keep up with, and everyone is feeling behind. Here’s the signal: the gap between what’s shipped and what’s documented. AI can help close it, but humans must stay in the loop, and teams need to decide who owns documentation and where that line now sits. - Adam Farren, Canvas Medical.

    One overlooked bottleneck is latency disguised as productivity. Especially with vibe coding and other AI methods, there will be more outputs, but not necessarily an increase in delivered value. Track flow efficiency: active work time versus end-to-end lead time. The gap reveals whether engineering or the delivery system is the bottleneck. AI is exposing the organizational gaps: process, data and other debts. - Neda Nia, Stibo Systems.

    Watch how long it takes a upcoming engineer to ship with confidence. That lag is the hidden cost of pipelines nobody questions anymore. AI speeds up commits, but a pipeline that only the original author understands isn’t fast; it’s fragile. Time to confident ship is the signal that exposes it. - Marc Fischer, Dogtown Media LLC.

    The hidden problem is who understands a change after it ships. Changes went up, but context went down. The signal is how many people get pulled into an incident before anyone can name what caused it. Count the Slack threads, not the deploys. One person answering every time means your pipeline is fast and your knowledge is a single point of failure. - Sanjay Gidwani, KOSMOS.

    Every pipeline reports what it found. Almost none report what it found again. AI assistants generate from patterns, so recurring flaws reproduce at machine speed. The signal is recurrence by weakness class, team and pipeline stage. Scan counts show volume; recurrence highlights whether you’re improving. A high number in one team is a skills gap; a high number everywhere is systemic: an insecure default or a copied prompt. - Andrea Scaduto, SecureFlag.

    Sources indicate that one hidden problem is work accumulating between development, testing and deployment. Teams may appear productive while releases slow down due to bottlenecks and rework. Tracking cycle time from code commit to production, alongside deployment frequency and failed releases, helps reveal where delays occur. Making these signals visible enables teams to address root causes and deliver software faster and more reliably. - Harsh Jangid, Coozmoo Digital Solutions.

    A pipeline can look healthy while teams work around it. Hotfixes, skipped checks and manual deploys happen under pressure and rarely appear on dashboards. Track the bypass rate: the share of production changes that skipped a standard check or were deployed by hand. A rising rate shows teams have stopped trusting the pipeline, which is the real problem to fix. - Venkatesh Sankaran, Saguna Consulting Services LLC.

    One hidden problem is validation debt. A delivery pipeline can stay green while teams repair data or reconcile outputs by hand. In large analytics programs, I have seen those workarounds survive several releases before surfacing as production defects. Track post-deployment reconciliation exceptions per release. A rising rate demonstrates the pipeline is passing code while shifting quality work downstream. - Govinda Rao Banothu, Cognizant Technology Solutions.

    Measure what one push now costs in model calls. Pipelines invoke AI on every commit for review, test generation and summaries, and that spend lands on the pipeline rather than on any team. At Google, we tracked compute cost per job the way we tracked latency. Track cost per merged change the same way. If it climbs while merge volume holds flat, your automation is getting more expensive at the same work. - Prashant Jalan, Guickly.

    Sources indicate that one hidden problem is accumulating risk from unresolved vulnerabilities and skipped quality checks as code moves through the delivery pipeline. Make it visible by tracking security findings, defect escape rates and rework at each stage. These signals help teams identify bottlenecks early, prevent production incidents and balance delivery speed with reliability. - Deepali Kaushik, NBCUniversal.

    Measure deployment frequency broken down by team, not just by pipeline. Aggregate metrics make the organization look healthier than it is. When you break frequency down by team, outliers become visible: one team shipping daily while another hasn’t deployed in three weeks. That gap rarely means the slow team has nothing to ship. It usually means something in their path has quietly stopped them. Aggregate metrics hide it. Team-level visibility surfaces it. - Dan Haiem, AppMakers USA.

    One hidden problem is flaky tests. Engineers learn to hit retry by reflex, so real failures slip through as noise, and the lost time never reveals up anywhere. The signal is the pass-on-retry rate: the share of runs that fail and then pass on the same commit with no code change. Track it per test and alert when it rises. - Srinivas Chippagiri, Salesforce Inc.

    It has been revealed that one hidden problem is the growing cost of change. Teams celebrate faster deployments while overlooking how much effort it takes to make even a small modification safely. Track the time from code completion to production, including rework, failed tests and approvals. If that time keeps growing, you’re not accelerating delivery. You’re accumulating friction disguised as progress. - Emma McGrattan, Actian.

    Jensen Huang Is Back as Nvidia CEO

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.
    • In a recent development, the stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago, and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him.
    • “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” stated recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.

    In a recent development, the stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago, and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.

    “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” stated recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.

    According to recent reports, in that announcement the board noted it was “satisfied with respect to Mr Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia,” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”.

    “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

    Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.

    “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

    According to recent reports, the day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.

    It has been revealed that in the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.

    In a recent development, huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which mentioned during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.

    Industry observers note that president Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a major lesson.”.

    Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with a Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.

    Recent findings suggest that huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The Latest York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.

    Alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI manufacturer that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm, and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.

    According to recent reports, huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the manufacturer was primarily known within the gaming community. It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphic processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.

    Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first ever organization to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.

    #142374. Five Ways AI Has Changed The Case For Modernizing Legacy Manufacturing Systems

    Five Ways AI Has Changed The Case For Modernizing Legacy Manufacturing Systems

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dimitar Dimitrov is the founder and Managing Partner at Accedia, a leading European AI & Custom Software Development Tech giant.
    • ​Your company may still depend on plant, warehouse or warranty systems built 20 or more years ago.
    • Most delays have two causes: Nobody knows what the old code does, and estimates for changing it are unreliable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dimitar Dimitrov is the founder and Managing Partner at Accedia, a leading European AI & Custom Software Development Tech giant.

    ​Your company may still depend on plant, warehouse or warranty systems built 20 or more years ago. For those systems, AI has changed the case for replacing them. AI tools can now document what that software does and map how its parts connect before you approve a budget.

    Most delays have two causes: Nobody knows what the old code does, and estimates for changing it are unreliable. Research indicates that enterprises spend 30% of IT budgets on modernization, yet only three in 10 have modernized their core applications. Each year of delay also leaves fewer people who understand how these systems work.

    Based on our recent delivery work at Accedia, I no longer advise manufacturers to fund a long discovery phase before legacy work can be estimated. AI now produces much of that analysis at the start of a project, so the estimate can be built on top of it.

    Sources indicate that AI-assisted legacy modernization in manufacturing is the use of AI to document and map the code of old plant systems before engineers change them. It shows how the parts of each system depend on each other and which code no longer runs. Engineers then replace the system in stages while it stays in use and remain accountable for every change.

    AI can document legacy manufacturing software by reading the source code and describing the purpose and connections of each part in plain language. An AWS case study from March 2026 indicates this at Toyota Motor Europe, which runs over 70 custom applications on legacy mainframes. The developers who know the languages behind those applications are retiring.

    With Deloitte and AWS, Toyota used AI to document two of the 10 modules in its warranty application. That application contains over 1.3 million lines of code. Toyota’s remaining experts checked a sample of the output against the code and confirmed its business rules, which led to a production rollout.

    For a CIO, this means the modernization decision no longer depends on what a few long-serving specialists remember. I believe documentation is the step manufacturers should fund first because every later decision depends on it.

    AI now surfaces hidden dependencies and unused code before anyone sets the scope. Finding them by hand made scoping slow and expensive.

    In a recent development, around 30% of our application development projects in the last 12 to 18 months involved AI-assisted legacy work, according to Accedia’s 2026 AI Delivery Report. Manufacturing and automotive clients were among the main beneficiaries. In those projects, the dependency map was the most valuable output, showing which parts could change without affecting the rest. The map is now the first deliverable we expect on any legacy engagement.

    Once AI has mapped the system, each component can be replaced while production continues. Until recently, only large programs could afford the analysis this approach needs. However, AI has made it affordable for smaller plant systems, too.

    Recent findings suggest that across our legacy projects, most regulated clients would not accept a single large migration while operations kept running. Working in stages also means many small releases, each raising the question of who signs off on code that AI helped write.

    AI tools are now standard on most of our projects. Senior engineers remain accountable for architecture, security and quality decisions, no matter how much code AI wrote. I recommend setting the same rule before the first component goes live and naming one person responsible for each change.

    Industry observers note that legacy languages are no longer the main barrier because current AI tools can read and map code written in VB6, Windows Forms and early .NET. Together with Java applications from the same period, they make up most of the AI-assisted modernization work we have delivered recently.

    Industry observers note that in my experience, a system’s technology mix matters more to the effort than the age of its code. A system built on a single technology can be simpler to modernize than a newer one that combines several. When our engineers review a legacy scope, their first question is how many languages and platforms the system uses. Systems connected to production equipment need more effort because each connection must be tested against the real machines.

    Sources indicate that AI has moved the main risk from the code to the business reasons behind it, which only plant staff know. Plant software often contains rules that look unnecessary, such as a short pause before a command reaches one particular machine. The code demonstrates the rule but not why it exists, so AI may treat it as safe to change and cause problems on the production line.

    According to recent reports, when we upgraded a warehouse system that a large U.S. food producer’s plant had used since the 1990s, our team made regular site visits. We needed to see the business rules and operating requirements that the code could not explain.

    Before changing any component, have plant staff review the AI’s description and turn their corrections into tests. On one recent project, the AI that wrote tests worked from the requirements and never saw the source code. Its tests described what the business needed, while tests generated from old code tend to treat that code’s existing errors as correct.

    In a recent development, manufacturing technology leaders should pick the first component of their oldest plant system to replace and name who signs off on its AI-written code. Both decisions are now realistic because AI addresses the two main reasons for waiting: missing documentation and unreliable estimates. Bring both to your next budget review with a date for plant staff to check what the AI has documented.

    Asked on Reddit: I Lost My Job; What Should I Do First?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A Redditor recently shared that they were struggling to decide which financial steps to take first after a job loss.
    • Sources indicate that should they withdraw money from retirement savings to have more cash on hand — but pay an early withdrawal penalty?
    • Many users responded with good ideas: File for unemployment, try to avoid tapping into retirement savings, and cut expenses as much as possible.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Redditor recently shared that they were struggling to decide which financial steps to take first after a job loss.

    Sources indicate that should they withdraw money from retirement savings to have more cash on hand — but pay an early withdrawal penalty? Or is it better to rely on the severance payout to handle expenses?

    Many users responded with good ideas: File for unemployment, try to avoid tapping into retirement savings, and cut expenses as much as possible.

    For more ideas, I asked three financial experts how to manage money in the immediate aftermath of job loss.

    Recent findings suggest that while it’s tempting to make quick decisions about tapping into a retirement fund or selling a house, it’s better to wait on any big moves, notes Parker Wine, retirement planning advisor at the financial firm Daniel A. White & Associates in Lewes, Delaware.

    Sources indicate that that’s because you need time to digest the situation and weigh the pros and cons of different options, he says. “People can get impulsive and panic, and it’s usually a bad thing to make decisions when you’re panicking,” he says.

    Take your time, get second opinions and think through all of your options first, Wine suggests.

    If you’re fortunate enough to receive a severance package, wait to sign it until you’ve reviewed it carefully and understand all of the details, claims John Rafferty, partner and investment advisor representative at Solomon Financial in Carmel, Indiana.

    For example, make sure you know about your health insurance options, such as whether you’ll receive insurance through COBRA or need to take out a newly introduced policy in the health insurance marketplace.

    Filing for unemployment and checking into any other available workplace benefits — such as help with your upcoming job search — is also an important part of understanding what support to expect in the weeks and months ahead, Rafferty adds.

    Creating a bare-bones budget stripped of “extras” like restaurant meals or travel can help the severance payment last as long as possible, Rafferty says.

    “Now that you don’t have income coming in, ask yourself, ‘How much can I spend and where?’”.

    You might be able to cut back on entertainment costs, coffee runs and clothing purchases, for example.

    It has been revealed that at the same time, it’s important to prioritize the essentials like mortgage payments, rent, utilities and food. Rafferty recommends calling your mortgage company, utilities provider and any other lenders to ask if they have a hardship program for those experiencing financial challenges.

    Opting in could give you more time to pay your bills or temporarily lower payments.

    It has been revealed that it’s hard to stick to a budget that eliminates all entertainment, so Rafferty suggests finding enjoyable activities that come with a low price tag. Hiking, discovering a latest park and participating in free community events are all ways to enjoy downtime on a budget.

    “Having that release is mentally a massive thing so you can stay prepared for the job search,” he claims. “Otherwise, it’s easy to get down and feel negative, and we need things to help us feel positive.”.

    Similarly, connecting with friends and family during this time is crucial, notes Laura Adams, accredited financial counselor and financial coach in Wilmington, North Carolina.

    People often feel a sense of shame or embarrassment after job loss, and Adams encourages people to talk about their feelings and ask for help if needed. “Financial shame can cause us to make emotional rather than confident financial decisions,” she notes.

    Starting some kind of side hustle to bring in extra cash can also help bridge the gap between the job loss and your next job, Wine indicates. Substitute teaching, working at a local public golf course and driving for a rideshare service are all options he’s seen people try.

    Doing something new also helps stave off boredom while unemployed, but he cautions that you’ll still owe taxes on any side income you bring in, so plan accordingly.

    All three financial experts also emphasized that a job loss is easier to handle with an emergency savings fund you can turn to, and suggested building one up — ideally three to six months’ worth of expenses. But starting small helps, too — while employed, if possible.

    The Redditor who posted the question mentioned that, like many Americans, they lacked emergency savings. This added urgency to the question of what to prioritize.

    Reddit is an online forum where consumers share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like how to deal with job loss, so we sifted through Reddit forums to get a pulse check. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

    Addas a preferred source on Google.

    #142371. From Reactive To Cognitive: Rethinking The NOC Around The Scorecard

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (731 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    From Reactive To Cognitive: Rethinking The NOC Around The Scorecard

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Arunava Sen - Director Solutions Engineering, Thought Leader, Intrapreneur, Evangelist, Problem Solver and a Curious Mind.
    • Traditionally, network operations centers (NOCs) were reactive, supporting customers only after problems arose.
    • Industry observers note that despite decades of investment in automation, monitoring, observability and IT service management (ITSM), many enterprises still operate with fragmented workflows, multiple escalation layers, reactive decision-making and heavy dependence on human intervention.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Arunava Sen - Director Solutions Engineering, Thought Leader, Intrapreneur, Evangelist, Problem Solver and a Curious Mind.

    Traditionally, network operations centers (NOCs) were reactive, supporting customers only after problems arose. Over time, they became proactive, with “Mean Time to Respond” taking center stage, and now they are becoming predictive, or cognitive. First came bot-driven automation, where human intent was translated through engines and grounded in relevant CLIs, observability or configurability. Next came agentic workers, built for network queries, incidents, trouble tickets, inventory and more.

    Industry observers note that despite decades of investment in automation, monitoring, observability and IT service management (ITSM), many enterprises still operate with fragmented workflows, multiple escalation layers, reactive decision-making and heavy dependence on human intervention. So the question is how we improve Net Promoter Score (NPS) across the board, whether for internal developers, end customers or assurance teams. In short, how do we improve the holistic experience?

    With Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations, agents became smarter through open LLMs and third-party resources. We introduced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which sat at the center of these grounding mechanisms and worked well. But we became so absorbed in these advances that the conversation turned into one about tools.

    Sources indicate that to confuse matters further, application performance monitoring (APM) and observability frameworks crowded the discussion. We went from human-driven desks to micro robot-driven workflows, which is no small feat. But before we congratulate ourselves, the real questions remain. How does deploying this infrastructure improve an organization’s balanced scorecard? What do we do with the engineers who supported these systems for so long? Do we need to re-skill them? How do we manage governance, accountability and risk? How do we make the infrastructure more intelligent? How do we leverage existing APM tools and infrastructure as code (IaC)? Who is the executive sponsor? What’s our fail-fast strategy? Eventually, all of these questions boil down to the balanced scorecard.

    Is this the way to create better NPS, faster turnaround time (TAT), lower MTTR and less management overhead? The tools are the ingredients and recipes, but the metrics we are solving for the business are the food on the table.

    Industry observers note that for a while, core semantics mattered for episodic and procedural memory, but then the need arose for semantics bundled with adjacencies. The intent was to ground queries as well as possible, in the shortest time, with near-zero hallucinations and no extra tools. Can we reduce mean time to respond by 30%? Can we improve first call resolution by 50%? Can we measure retention rate? If we do this right every day, there could come a time when there are no tickets, and we will have redefined CX.

    According to recent reports, this is where knowledge graphs built on ontology frameworks such as RDF/OWL could be one option. As we define this better, we may see the emergence of VKN (vector and knowledge graphs, similar to Graph RAG). The ontology could cover networks or anything else, but it would go beyond vector databases, helping queries get processed and grounded without many iterations. Yet while we have vectors and now knowledge graphs, how do we deal with people? Remember, our key questions at the beginning were about the balanced scorecard, and NPS and people are strong indicators on it.

    According to recent reports, I believe we will still need engineers for Day 0 (assessment) and Day 1 (program management and governance). This could also mean shifting the traditional desk model from Levels 1/2/3 to just two sets of engineers: a “front end” and an “escalation end.” The front end performs Day 0 and Day 1. The escalation end provides tool support and integrations, creates and maintains vectors and graphs, uses agent orchestration tools, and keeps the configurability and observability infrastructure clean and lean. Everyone elevates their tasks and skills.

    In a recent development, the way I envisage it, operational designs will have humans at the front, architecting and governing the scorecard metrics; AI agents, MCP, RAG, orchestrators, ontologies and databases in the middle, enabling those metrics; and human experts at the back end, where cognition is the only thing that matters. Other options may exist or emerge, but this approach will likely serve enterprise utilization and customer experience better, and therefore retention.

    Its next weight-loss drug, Retatrutide, is hotly anticipated for its triple-agonist approach, which is expected to exceed the weight-loss results of Zepbound. The company is also targeting less affluent customers with a lower-cost GLP pill called Foundayo, which it sells directly to consumers.

    It has been revealed that besides GLP-1s, Lilly is working on a small interfering RNA therapeutic targeting lipoprotein(a) for the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in patients with elevated lipoprotein(a) levels. Analysts believe it will be a blockbuster ($1 billion or more in lifetime revenue) if approved.

    Sources indicate that lilly shares come at a premium, but that is a bet on future growth. Vertex is a compelling addition to one's portfolio, too, especially at a cheaper valuation than Lilly. But the explosion of GLP-1s seems still in the early innings, making Lily the pick for 2027.

    With Mortgage Rates Rising, Should You Hibernate Until Spring?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.
    • The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov.
    • It has been revealed that A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

    The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

    It has been revealed that A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

    It has been revealed that one bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

    Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

    Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) revealed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

    According to recent reports, while CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

    To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

    According to recent reports, even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how rapidly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

    If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

    In a recent development, but latest data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

    According to recent reports, pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

    “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

    Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

    Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

    Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.).

    Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

    Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

    #142366. The 42-Point Lie Your Dashboards Are Telling You

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (822 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    The 42-Point Lie Your Dashboards Are Telling You

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Gunter Ollmann is CTO of Cobalt, and brings decades of experience and innovation to the forefront of information security.
    • ​Let’s be honest about what a 42-point gap actually means.
    • Sources indicate that ​When you ask security leaders whether their teams are consistently hitting remediation service level agreements (SLAs), 57% say yes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Gunter Ollmann is CTO of Cobalt, and brings decades of experience and innovation to the forefront of information security.

    ​Let’s be honest about what a 42-point gap actually means.

    Sources indicate that ​When you ask security leaders whether their teams are consistently hitting remediation service level agreements (SLAs), 57% say yes. When you ask the practitioners doing the actual remediation work, only 15% agree. That data point comes from my organization’s “State of Pentesting 2026” report, and it deserves more than a footnote. A 42-point gap between leadership perception and practitioner reality is not a rounding error, but a governance failure hiding in plain sight.

    ​The instinct, when faced with a number like that, is to question one of the two figures. Either leadership is deluded, or practitioners are pessimistic. That framing lets you dismiss the problem rather than confront it. The harder interpretation (and likely the correct one) is that both groups are reporting what they actually see. The gap is the finding.​.

    According to recent reports, before deciding which read to trust, consider who lives with the consequences. When a significant AI security incident hits, 78% of security teams absorb the internal blame. Not the executive who approved the dashboard or the leader who cited the 57% figure in the board presentation; the team. The same team telling you the SLAs aren’t being met.

    In a recent development, that asymmetry of accountability should inform how you weigh their assessment. The people closest to the exposure, who will be held responsible when it materializes, are telling you something different from what the summary layer is reporting. Standard governance structures are filtering out the hard read and replacing it with something more presentable. That is not a data problem. That is an incentive problem.​.

    The change in perceptions over one year are striking. The trajectory in the data and lack of AI preparedness are what should unsettle any executive paying attention.

    In 2025, our research indicated 64% of organizations felt well-equipped to handle AI security challenges. That figure has dropped to 51%, which is a 13-point decline in a single year. Over the same period, calls for a strategic pause on AI adoption rose 13 points, reaching 61%, while 82% of teams report investing more in AI security than they did a year ago.​.

    If you read these facts together and conclude that your team is underperforming, you are missing the point entirely. You are looking at people working harder against a target they can see clearly and that leadership has not defined honestly.

    It has been revealed that ​Think of it this way: a construction crew pouring concrete into the wrong foundation does not fix the structural problem by pouring more concrete. Effort without accurate situational awareness does not compound into readiness. Eventually, it just exhausts the people doing the work.

    In a recent development, an organization cannot indefinitely ask practitioners to own the risk, override their read of it and expect them to keep showing up at full capacity. That is not a culture critique. Instead, it’s a basic observation about how attrition works.

    ​The gap between what leadership reports and what practitioners see is not static. It is a daily friction that practitioners feel acutely, because they are the ones watching the organization act on a cleaner story than the one in front of them. The people with the sharpest read and the most career options will feel that friction first, and they will act on it first.

    In a recent development, ​The organizations that close this gap and build their remediation governance around what practitioners actually observe will systematically out-execute the ones managing from the executive summary. Not because they try harder, but because they are solving the actual problem instead of a flattering approximation of it.

    ​The blind spot was never in your stack. It was in your reporting structure. The 42-point gap is telling you exactly where to look.

    To close this gap from the ground up, security practitioners can start with four concrete steps:.

    1. Audit your metrics. Don’t rely solely on automated dashboard rollups. Track actual time-to-remediate against operational realities to surface hidden friction points to management.

    Sources indicate that 2. Standardize reporting. Establish a formal process for flagging SLA discrepancies early, documenting systemic blockers (e.g., lack of context, tool noise) alongside the raw vulnerability count.

    3. Establish realistic AI risk baselines. Require explicit operational definitions for “AI readiness” within your team rather than accepting vague executive benchmarks.

    4. Push for shared risk ownership. Ensure remediation SLAs are tied to business-unit resource commitments rather than letting security practitioners absorb sole accountability for unmitigated risk.

    When security teams and executive leadership share the same ground-level truth, risk governance stops being a flattering story and becomes a real operational advantage.​.

    • One has a hard deadline, and the other is heading into its favorite time of year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 23, 2026 at 10:45AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than American Express ›.

    Industry observers note that berkshire Hathaway (BRKB +0.58%)(BRKA +0.58%) filed its latest list of stock holdings this week, and I skipped straight to two lines. Coca-Cola (KO -1.08%): 400 million shares. American Express (AXP +1.90%): 151.6 million shares.

    It has been revealed that those numbers barely ever move. Berkshire completed its Coca-Cola purchase in 1994 and essentially finished buying Amex in 1995. Greg Abel, who now runs Berkshire, named both among the businesses "we understand well, have a high regard for their leaders, and expect will compound over decades." Warren Buffett remarked it best back in 1988, the year he started buying Coke: "Our favorite holding period is forever.".

    I'd buy both before December. One has a hard deadline, and the other is heading into its favorite time of year.

    Coca-Cola will pay its next quarterly dividend to shareholders of record on Dec. 1. That makes Dec. 1 the ex-dividend date, too, so you'd need to buy by the close on Monday, Nov. 30. One payment won't make anyone rich, but Buffett wrote in 2022 that Berkshire's Coca-Cola dividend grew every year after 1994, "just as certain as birthdays.".

    What I like more is how Coca-Cola is growing. CEO Henrique Braun stated on the earnings call that after visiting markets around the world, "affordability is working" and "both Zero Sugar and Original Taste are recruiting consumers." That means 500ml Super Cans plus low-cost single-serve packs in places like Vietnam and South Africa, while Coca-Cola Zero Sugar grew 16% last quarter. Closer to home, Braun pointed to strong volume from fairlife protein shakes, Powerade, and smartwater, so this isn't just a soda story anymore.

    According to recent reports, coca-Cola has now raised its full-year outlook three quarters in a row, but CNBC noted demand in its home market has been lackluster. Braun still sounded confident about North America, saying the price increases sticking there show "that the brands have the equity and the right to take price." That's pricing power.

    There's also a long-running tax fight, with CFO John Murphy saying Coca-Cola is managing its balance sheet "as we await a court decision related to our ongoing dispute with the IRS." And the stock sits near its 52-week high, so this isn't a bargain buy.

    NYSE · As of 11:45 AM ET 11/23/26.

    American Express (AXP +1.90%) is technically a financial stock, but it lives and dies on consumer spending.

    According to recent reports, its "before December" moment is Small Business Saturday on Nov. 28. "Since creating Small Business Saturday in 2010, we've encouraged consumers to discover and support the businesses in their neighborhoods," remarked Chief Marketing Officer Elizabeth Rutledge in a press release.

    The pitch to shop owners is simple: Amex says the average U.S. card member spends 3 times as much as people carrying cards on other networks.

    The bigger story is who's signing up. CEO Steve Squeri remarked latest card members are "predominantly millennials and Gen Z," and a year after Amex refreshed its Platinum card, CFO Christophe Le Caillec said, "Spend retention remains at 99%.".

    In a recent development, amex keeps piling on reasons to stay, from a new Airbnb partnership to Resy Rewards, rolled out this week in New York City, which gives card members extra points for dining at participating restaurants. "Rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table," remarked Resy CEO Pablo Rivero. That's a network effect in action, with more diners drawing in more restaurants.

    It hasn't been a spotless year. Regulators hit Amex with a consent order and a civil money penalty, and Squeri admitted, "The deficiencies cited in the consent order should not have occurred." It's also cutting about 5% of its workforce. And rivals like Chase, Citigroup, and Capital One are chasing the same wealthy customers, a fight Squeri expects to remain fierce because premium cardholders are such a profitable slice of the market.

    Berkshire never needed perfect years from either firm. Both have weathered recessions, fads, and plenty of rivals since the 1990s. What Berkshire needed was brands people kept choosing, decade after decade, and a buy-and-hold strategy patient enough to let the dividends pile up.

    Coca-Cola and Amex are still those brands, and I plan to own them the way Berkshire does.
